items.title: Stack, naming and format foundations
items.context: Settled with the developer on 2026-11-02 while building Phase 1.
items.decision: CLI is `dsheets` (name kept in internal/brand). Go; any web UI is served on localhost by the Go binary (`dsheets serve`) as plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step or framework. All sheet numbers are CEL doubles. Range keys such as `[18..35]` live in lookup data. Evidence is shown by default. Wording is domain- and org-neutral: 'target', never 'partner'; generic examples such as specs/order-checkout.
items.rationale: Developer's choices from the original handoff's open questions; the tool should read as usable within a team or across organisations. Don't re-ask these.

items.title: Cross-team model: one repository per team, a registry, follow main
items.context: Agreed and built 2026-11-03 (PR #1). Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-03-cross-repo-references-design.md; docs/repositories.md, docs/flows.md.
items.decision: Each team keeps its sheets and interfaces in its own repository; cross-team references (`alias:path`) are read-only and follow the default branch. A registry repository of git submodules lists the teams. `dsheets impact` tells a producing team, in its own pull request, which other teams' flows its change breaks. Only each team's sheets folder is fetched, shallow and sparse. Whether a failing check blocks a merge is the organisation's CI policy, not dsheets'.
items.rationale: Teams change signatures without meetings, assuming nobody consumes them; producers must learn what they break before merging.

items.title: Visual editor design
items.context: Agreed in conversation 2026-11-03; spec docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-03-visual-editor-design.md (mockups in the git-ignored .superpowers/brainstorm). Refines the 2026-11-02 call that slicing is done in flow.toml rather than by drag-and-drop: the flow panel now pins rows with form actions ('compute here'), still not drag-and-drop.
items.decision: One editor for everyone, turned on with `dsheets serve --edit`; edits happen on the existing sheet and flow pages through a side panel with live preview. Saves write only the changed TOML spans, keep comments and formatting byte-for-byte elsewhere, and are refused only for errors the edit introduces. Files reached through alias: are read-only. Out of scope for now: creating sheets or flows from scratch, CSV and case editing, renaming after first save, git operations, re-slicing flows on save.
items.rationale: Product managers should not edit TOML, and developers must find the editor faster than the TOML, not a simplified tool.

items.title: Build the visual editor next, starting with the TOML writer
items.context: Concierge session 2026-11-06. Alternatives weighed: PR diffs first (T-5: smaller, useful in reviews straight away; BACKLOG.md's suggested order put it first, but that was written an hour before the editor design was agreed); lists design first (T-8: the only open format question; T-1 is format-agnostic, so it can wait).
items.decision: Build the visual editor in four milestones (T-1 to T-4), starting with the comment-preserving TOML writer and file store (T-1), preceded by the editor's implementation plan. PR diffs (T-5) and the change-to-work project (T-6) follow the editor.
items.rationale: The design is agreed and only needs a plan; the editor is the point of Phase 2 (product managers authoring without TOML); the writer is the riskiest part and testable on its own; it can also back the formatter (T-7); and the spec sequences T-6 and PR diffs after the editor because they share one comparison.

items.title: Where the backlog lives
items.context: Hopback was added 2026-11-06 while the backlog lived in BACKLOG.md, which README links to in a public repository.
items.decision: Hopback holds the working backlog (status, ranks, decisions). BACKLOG.md stays as the public roadmap and is refreshed at milestones, not on every change.
items.rationale: One place for agents to track work across sessions, without breaking the public roadmap README points to.

items.title: Formatter scope: should dsheets fmt (T-7) normalise value text or only layout?
items.context: Raised when editor M1 merged (tomledit.Format re-lays out spans but keeps each value's text as written; the editor writes canonical text only for values it changed). Developer chose on 2026-11-06 to settle this when T-7 starts. Concierge recommended layout only.

options.name: Layout only
options.tradeoffs: key order, alignment, indentation; 0.10 stays 0.10 and hand-aligned decision tables keep their spacing. Free on tomledit.Format; identical to what the editor writes, so the two never disagree.

options.name: Layout and values
options.tradeoffs: fully uniform files, but hand-aligned decision-table cells lose their alignment (less readable in raw TOML) and tomledit needs a value-normalising mode.

items.decision: Layout only: dsheets fmt normalises key order, alignment and indentation, and keeps each value's text as written.
items.rationale: Free on tomledit.Format and identical to what the editor writes, so the two never disagree; hand-aligned decision tables keep their spacing and 0.10 stays 0.10.

items.title: Build editor M2 (T-2) next, starting with an independent review of M1
items.context: Concierge session 2026-11-06, after M1 (internal/store, internal/tomledit) merged as PR #2 with only a self-review. Alternatives weighed: T-7 formatter first (small; keeps editor diffs tight in repos not yet in canonical layout, but example files already are, so it does not block T-2); T-8 lists design first (only open format question; would avoid reworking RowData and panel forms, but it is a wide design conversation and nothing is blocked).
items.decision: Build T-2 next. Its first step is a fresh independent review (e.g. /code-review) of the M1 merge 9c5c18a, with fixes on the T-2 branch before plan Task 5. T-5 and T-6 review flags cleared (no scope change; they read committed content via store.Committed). T-7 stays flagged until its fmt-scope decision is made.
items.rationale: T-2 is the first milestone people can use, the reason for the editor (D-3, D-4); T-3 and T-4 depend on it; the plan already breaks it into tasks 5-9 with tests. M2 builds directly on tomledit, whose byte-for-byte guarantee is the editor's core promise, so a fresh review before building on it is cheap insurance.

items.title: Input rows may have reject conditions
items.context: The validator refuses [[row.reject]] on input rows (error reject-on-input: 'reject conditions belong on derived rows; add a derived row for the check'), and docs/format.md lists rejects for derived rows only. The rule dates from the first commit (86c264c) with no recorded reason. Raised while testing the M2 editor, which offers Add reject on input rows.
items.decision: Allow reject conditions on input rows.
items.rationale: Developer: logically input rows should also allow rejections; there is no reason they should not, and the restriction was probably overlooked when format.md was written. Input rows can already reject (a missing required input rejects with MISSING_INPUT).

items.title: Which rows may an input row's reject condition name?
items.context: Raised while building T-19 (PR #4, merged 615de84). As built, an input row's reject names rows directly (inputs have no uses) and may name any row, including derived ones, matching what an input's when already allows; the graph orders the input after them and the validator reports cycles. T-19's description could be read as 'the row itself and other inputs' only. Developer asked at the end of the session; not answered yet.

options.name: Any row (as built)
options.tradeoffs: consistent with an input's when; an input check may depend on a derived value, which delays reading that input until the value is computed.

options.name: The row itself and other inputs only
options.tradeoffs: keeps input checks about the request; needs a small extra validator check and a doc line.

items.decision: The row itself and other inputs only. An input row's reject may not name derived rows; a check that needs a derived value is written as a reject on that derived row.
items.rationale: Developer, 2026-11-08: if required, the user can write it in the derived row. Nothing is lost, because a derived row's reject can name anything in its uses. It avoids the cycle trap (an input reject naming a derived row that uses that input, such as subtotal -> discount) and keeps input rejects as checks on the request itself. An input's `when` may still name derived rows, because it decides whether the input is required at all. Neither specs/order-checkout nor examples/pieces/2-orders-team has an input reject today.

items.title: Editor: how an edit shows on the sheet before saving
items.context: T-17. The developer asked for a 'save in the panel'; clarified 2026-11-07 they meant an in-place visual update to review before the real Save, not a write. An 'Update sheet' button was built, then removed at the developer's request because the sheet already redraws when typing pauses.

options.name: Live redraw only
options.tradeoffs: the sheet redraws from the draft ~0.4s after typing stops; no panel button

options.name: Live redraw plus an Update sheet button
options.tradeoffs: redundant with the live redraw

items.decision: Live redraw only, no panel button; Save in the bottom bar is the only write
items.rationale: Developer: the button adds nothing when the sheet already updates in 0.4s

items.title: Loose ends not put in the backlog (2026-11-08)
items.context: The concierge offered to add carried-over items from past handoffs to the backlog. The developer added two (broken-sheet repair, editor polish) and chose not to add the others.
items.decision: Not in the backlog: an independent /code-review of PRs #3-#7, and the tomledit bug where a comment inside an empty [] list attaches to the next item.
items.rationale: The developer's choice in the 2026-11-08 concierge session; no reason given. Don't offer them again unless something changes.

items.title: Show every decision table as a rule table; drop the 2-input cross-tab
items.context: The developer found the sheet page's 2-input decision table (loyalty_tier: corner 'is_member ╲ customer_years', one input down the side, one across the top) hard to understand, and thought it could not show more than two inputs. The format has no such limit; internal/render/rule.go tableHTML draws 1 input as an inline list, 2 inputs as a cross-tab (grid2D), and 3+ inputs (or a too-large grid) as a rule table (compactTable). The T-3 editor uses the rule-list form, so a cross-tab view would show the same table in two shapes.

options.name: Rule table + grid toggle
options.tradeoffs: rule table by default, cross-tab as an optional view for 2-input tables

options.name: Rule table only
options.tradeoffs: drop the cross-tab; every table looks the same

options.name: Keep grid, label it
options.tradeoffs: cross-tab for 2 inputs with clear axis labels

items.decision: Rule table only: one row per rule, one column per input, then the result column and the hit policy, for every decision table, matching the file and the T-3 editor. The 2-input cross-tab (grid2D) goes. Done in T-3's first PR.
items.rationale: Developer's choice (2026-11-08): one consistent shape that works for any number of inputs and matches what the editor edits. The cross-tab's one advantage (seeing gaps and overlaps) is not needed as a separate view because T-3 flags gaps and overlaps while editing.

items.title: T-3 editor: how table cells are edited and what the case list shows
items.context: Asked at the start of T-3 (2026-11-08).

options.name: Free-text cells
options.tradeoffs: type what the file holds (>= 2, -, Gold, true)

options.name: Operator + value
options.tradeoffs: a dropdown and a value box per cell

items.decision: Free-text cells. The case list shows, per case, the values of the rows the selected row uses and its result (or why there is none).
items.rationale: Developer's choice; free text is fastest for people who know the format, and seeing the inputs explains each result without leaving the panel.

items.title: Keep values_file CSVs once lookups can hold multi-key values inline?
items.context: Raised by the developer on 2026-11-08 during T-3: lookup data really lives in a database, so the repo only needs design-time sample values, and an editable table in the panel is enough. See the task for inline multi-key values.

options.name: Remove values_file
options.tradeoffs: one way to write lookup data, all of it editable in the panel; the example CSVs move into sheet.toml; any sheet using values_file must be migrated (only this repo's examples today)

options.name: Keep both, the editor writes inline
options.tradeoffs: nothing breaks; CSV-backed lookups stay read-only in the editor; two ways to write the same thing

items.title: Brainstorm: how should dsheets handle database-backed lookups?
items.context: Developer, 2026-11-08, during T-3's lookup form: in real code lookup data lives in a database, so values_file CSVs in the repo are an outlier. To be settled in a brainstorming session, not decided yet. Questions to cover: what a lookup's design-time values are for (cases, validation of gaps and overlaps, the sheet page); whether they live inline in sheet.toml (multi-key with ranges, as [row.table] has), in CSVs, or are read from the real database or a snapshot (see T-14); whether values_file stays; how the editor shows and edits them. Today: inline values take one key; specs/order-checkout's zone and shipping_fee use CSVs; the editor shows CSV data read-only (branch editor-m3-lookups).

items.title: Flow editor: what the panel offers for warning (⚠) and rowless missing (✕) marks
items.context: T-4 planning, 2026-11-08. The spec's 'add field or map to an existing field' fits ✕ marks; ⚠ means the field exists but does not fit (optional when always needed, wrong type, enum). Some ✕ marks have no row (a required field nothing produces, e.g. payment-request currency).

options.name: Map + fix the field
options.tradeoffs: map to another field, plus 'make required' and 'change type' on interface files in this repository; enum mismatches read-only

options.name: Map only
options.tradeoffs: as the spec says; fixes stay hand edits

options.name: Read-only
options.tradeoffs: only ✕ marks get actions

items.decision: ⚠: map to another field, plus 'make required' (optional when always needed) and 'change type' (type mismatch) on interface files in this repository; enum mismatches stay read-only. Rowless ✕ marks stay in the To agree list, not handled in M4. T-4 ships as one PR.
items.rationale: Developer's choice. Enum fixes are usually a send map on the sheet; rowless gaps are usually fixed by a new row on the sheet page.

items.title: Should dsheets diff prefer the registry's followed branch as its default base?
items.context: T-5 resolves the default base from git (origin/HEAD, origin/main, origin/master, main, master). dsheets impact instead uses the branch the registry follows. Raised in the T-5 design review; left open in PR #13.

options.name: Yes, registry branch first
options.tradeoffs: diff and impact never disagree about the base; needs the registry resolver reachable from diff

options.name: No, git chain only
options.tradeoffs: diff stays usable with no registry; two commands may pick different bases

items.decision: Yes: dsheets diff prefers the registry's followed branch as its default base, falling back to the git chain (origin/HEAD, origin/main, origin/master, main, master) when there is no registry.
items.rationale: diff and impact should never disagree about the base. Developer chose this on 2026-11-13.

items.title: T-6: requirements come from comparing the flow analysed at base and at head
items.context: Developer approved the design in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-13-requirements-design.md on 2026-11-14.
items.decision: `dsheets requirements <flow>` compares flow.Analyze at the base and at head and writes a flat, dependency-ordered list per team: Compute, Send, Receive, Carry, Schema. diff.Report only supplies before/after text and the label filter. dsheets does not group requirements into tickets and does not order teams against each other.
items.rationale: diff.Report sees only the repository being diffed, cannot tell a new Send from an existing one and has no Carry; the analysis already resolves the flow across repositories. Ticket grouping and cross-team coordination belong to the team lead or PM.

items.title: T-6: --apply writes interface edits only, on a pushed new branch in the owner repo
items.context: Interfaces are the minimum every team has; teams document at different depths.
items.decision: `--apply` makes a sparse shallow clone of the owner repo's dsheets folder, cuts a new branch (default dsheets/<flow>, or --branch alias=name) from the branch the registry names for that repo, edits the interface with tomledit, commits and pushes it (--no-push to stop locally). It never touches existing branches, never force-pushes, never pushes to the default branch, and does not open the pull request. A team's own internal sheets or docs are updated by the team; dsheets neither writes them nor lists an item.
items.rationale: The interface change rides in the owner's development PR with the code so a reviewer sees both. The developer renames the branch and starts work. No platform API is needed.

items.title: T-6: the flow pull request merges after development; no shared branch names
items.context: Teams use their own branch naming (initials, sprint, user story, description).
items.decision: The PM's flow PR stays open as the agreement and merges last, after the owner PRs, so every alias is read from its followed branch and no branch lookup in other repositories is needed. Requirements are recomputed from git and shrink as owner PRs merge. PRs are linked by stable requirement ids, a record file written by --apply (changes/<label>.md) that survives squash, and a printed PR description; branch names and trailers are never relied on.
items.rationale: Keeps main describing what is live and keeps the diff recomputable; works with any team's naming and any merge style.

items.title: Requirements close from the owners' own sheets on the branch the registry follows (approach A)
items.context: T-30 brainstorm, 2026-11-14, developer decisions. A merged owner sheet is taken to mean the team's code is merged and working; dsheets never reads code. Done items drop out of the list like Schema items, with a count. A team with no sheet shows 'not documented', separate from open, and does not block the flow merge. Approaches considered: A read the owner's sheets (chosen), B re-run flow analysis on the owner's flow, C teams list finished ids in a record file. The rule from the PM's sheet travels with each Compute item. There is no release-order guard: merged is not released, ordering between teams is a release concern, not dsheets'. Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-14-requirements-done-check-design.md.
items.decision: Approach A: an item is done when the owner's own sheets on the registry-followed branch show the work; no sheet means not documented (never done, never blocking); done items are hidden and counted; Compute items carry the rule; no ordering guard between teams.
items.rationale: Matches the developer's assumption that a merged sheet means merged, working code, covers teams that document at different depths without wrongly marking work done, and needs no extra file or flow in the owner's repo. Option C was rejected as a second mechanism; B only works for teams with flows.

items.title: T-30 fixes from the whole-branch review: boundary-aware matching, never close on a guess
items.context: Final review of T-30 found false-close cases; fixes made 2026-11-14 and committed. Recorded so the matching rules are not loosened later.
items.decision: Send closes only at its boundary (call request by a send to that stage, anything else by the sheet's own target); Receive only from the request, or call.<stage>.<field> for a response, never config, db or context; the rule comparison covers every non-label field of the row; items owned by the flow's own repository, and absence-evidence when a sheet cannot be read, are not documented; every repository of a team is read.
items.rationale: The spec's anti-goal: an item must never close on a guess. Each rule was reproduced as a false done in the Acme sandbox before it was fixed.

items.title: Boundary agreement: a PM row at an intermediate boundary is binding
items.context: T-32 design (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-21-boundary-agreement-design.md). Team sheets are checked against the PM's sheet by running the PM's cases and comparing values at boundaries. Question: when the PM's sheet has a row carried on a boundary between two teams (Acme: shipping_fee on quote-response.fee), and the teams split the work differently (Shipping halves the fee for Silver instead of Orders), is that inner value compared?

options.name: A binding
options.tradeoffs: the inner value is part of the contract; the item stays open until the PM changes the sheet

options.name: B not compared
options.tradeoffs: only outer boundaries are checked

options.name: C warning
options.tradeoffs: report the difference but close the item when everything downstream agrees

items.decision: A: binding. A PM row carried on any boundary, outer or between two teams, is compared; teams choose the split freely only where the PM's sheet has no row at the boundary between them, and otherwise ask the PM to change the sheet.
items.rationale: Developer's choice, 2026-11-21.

items.title: T-32: agree on behaviour at boundaries, checked by the PM's cases
items.context: T-32 brainstorm, 2026-11-21. The PM's sheet (intent) and the teams' sheets (implementation) describe the same logic at different granularity and drift; the T-30 done-check matches rule text, so it cannot close work written at a different granularity.

options.name: A one editor updates flow, sheet and schema together
B developers write only code; the sheet is generated from it
C keep rule-text matching and copy the PM's rule into team sheets
D boundary agreement checked by running the PM's cases

items.decision: D. Each file owns one thing (PM's sheet: intent and cases; flow: boundaries and the answering team per PM row, no logic; team sheets: all logic; interfaces: what crosses). A pin means the team answers for the value at its boundary. Done = verify passes (sheet matches code) and the PM's cases agree at the boundaries (code matches intent). Sheet first is the default; code first gets the same checks. See docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-21-boundary-agreement-design.md.
items.rationale: Approved by the developer, 2026-11-21. Keeps the slice meeting short, keeps logic out of the flow, lets team sheets be more detailed than the PM's, and works for sheet-first and code-first work.

items.title: T-35 plan calls: own-flow fallback and Send-only value check
items.context: Two choices in the boundary-agreement plan that the T-32 design does not cover. Developer confirmed both on 2026-11-21.
items.decision: (a) A team that has sheets but no own flow matching the boundary keeps the T-30 rule-text check, with the note 'checked by rule text: no flow of <team> joins <in> to <out>'. It does not report cannot tell. (b) Receive and Carry items stay structural. Only Send items get the value check by cases.
items.rationale: (a) Keeps the check that teams without a flow have today (TestRunClosesAnItemFromTheOwnersSheet). (b) Gating a Receive item on another team's values would make one team's item depend on another team's work.

items.title: Case checks: callee without a flow; Send when cases cannot tell
items.context: Two rulings made while building T-35, confirmed by the developer on 2026-11-21.
items.decision: (1) When a team calls a team that has no own flow, the caller's Compute items that depend on the call are not documented, not closed by rule text (D-22). D-25(a)'s rule-text fallback covers only the team that itself lacks a flow. (2) A Send item that is structurally done stays done when its cases cannot tell; only a differing case reopens it.
items.rationale: (1) The caller's values cannot be computed without the callee's answer, so closing by rule text would be a guess. Undocumented items do not block the flow. (2) The value itself is judged by the row's Compute item, so the Send item does not need to judge it again.

items.title: Next build: design section 6 (Requirements panel) before T-34
items.context: Concierge, 2026-11-21, after T-35 merged. T-34 (test middleware) had been the developer's pick right after T-32. Section 6 was in the T-32 design's delivery order but had no backlog task.
items.decision: Build section 6 next as T-37, starting with the T-36 fix in the same session. T-31 is folded into T-37. T-34 moves to after T-37.
items.rationale: Section 6 is already designed (needs a plan, not a brainstorm), reuses T-35's code while it is fresh, finishes the owner-facing loop of boundary agreement, and removes T-31. T-34 opens a new area (driving team code through adapters) and needs a full brainstorm. T-36 goes first because the panel turns cases green and a missing generated branch would make all green misleading.

items.title: T-37 plan calls beyond design section 6
items.context: Plan docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-22-requirements-panel.md; developer approved 2026-11-22.
items.decision: (1) --flow needs alias and @branch. (2) The PM's repository is fetched with full commit history, blob-less and sparse, so the change is compared with the merge-base. (3) Neighbour items show only through calls: a callee sees the caller's Compute/Send items whose row depends on a row carried by that call; handoff neighbours are not shown. (4) Single save is always on in serve --edit on a sheet; a save that still leaves a new flow error after unpinning is refused. (5) Reruns go in a separate /edit/requirements request after each check. (6) Rows producing fields: sending rows plus derived ancestors, inputs left out. (7) The PM change is read once at start and on Fetch again.
items.rationale: Developer: fine. Execution: subagent-driven.
